A.explanation: Gives $V = P/I = 500/0.5 = 1000\text{ V}$, not the $250\text{ V}$ mains supply.

B.explanation: Gives $V = P/I = 500/5.0 = 100\text{ V}$, not the $250\text{ V}$ mains supply.

C.explanation: Gives $V = P/I = 2500/0.1 = 25000\text{ V}$, far larger than the $250\text{ V}$ mains supply.

D.explanation: Gives $V = P/I = 2500/10 = 250\text{ V}$, matching the supply, with a realistic $2500\text{ W}$ kettle power.

hints: Notice the supply voltage is $250\text{ V}$ and each row pairs a power in $\text{W}$ with a current in $\text{A}$.
Recall $P = VI$ for an electrical heater, so any possible pair must satisfy $P/I = 250\text{ V}$.
Calculate $P/I$ for each row and consider that a mains kettle is typically a few kilowatts, near $2500\text{ W}$ rather than $0.1\text{ A}$ or $0.5\text{ A}$.
walkthrough: Identify the fixed quantity: the kettle operates at $V = 250\text{ V}$ from the mains supply.
State the governing relation for electrical power: $P = VI$, which can be rearranged to $V = P/I$ and $I = P/V$.

Test the power-current pairs for consistency with $250\text{ V}$: for $500\text{ W}$ the current should be $I = 500/250 = 2.0\text{ A}$, and for $2500\text{ W}$ it should be $I = 2500/250 = 10\text{ A}$.
Compare with the table: only $2500\text{ W}$ with $10\text{ A}$ gives $P/I = 2500/10 = 250\text{ V}$, while the other rows give $1000\text{ V}$, $100\text{ V}$ and $25000\text{ V}$.
Note this is also physically sensible because a mains kettle is a high-power heater of order $2$-$3\text{ kW}$. This is option D.
